picks.excerpt: This week's international roundup: German children's publisher Carlsen sues OpenAI with author Marc-Uwe Kling and illustrator Astrid Henn, saying ChatGPT generates Das NEINhorn-like stories, illustrations and even print-ready files with a fake ISBN and the publisher's logo; Brazil's Publitik launches an AI-agent book-market intelligence platform.
picks.rationale: Hardest news in the pool: a major German publisher and its star author sue OpenAI over ChatGPT emitting print-ready lookalike books complete with a fake ISBN and the house logo.

picks.excerpt: ALLi's Self-Publishing News for 13 August 2026 explains how the EU's new AI transparency rules — including watermarking and training-data disclosure — reach indie authors far outside Europe.
picks.rationale: Compliance news with extraterritorial teeth: watermarking and training-data disclosure obligations that indie authors outside the EU must plan for now.

picks.excerpt: As publishers sign LLM-training licences, microdeals and multi-territory rights deals, royalty and reporting transparency for authors is becoming table stakes. The piece argues rights systems, not goodwill, will decide whether AI licensing money reaches creators.
picks.rationale: Shifts the AI-licensing debate from whether deals happen to whether the money reaches authors — royalty reporting infrastructure as the decisive variable.

picks.excerpt: Indie author Nigel George argues writers hold more power over AI's trajectory than they think: set explicit boundaries on AI use, defend human copyright, and treat the model as a very sophisticated calculator rather than a collaborator.
picks.rationale: Freshest item in the pool and directly actionable — a concrete stance a writer can adopt tomorrow: draw the boundary, treat the model as a calculator, not a co-author.

picks.excerpt: A look at which publishing technologies — AI-assisted production, metadata and discovery tooling among them — are worth piloting versus scaling across a house's workflow.
picks.rationale: The pilot-versus-scale distinction is the practical question inside publishing houses right now; useful roadmap framing rather than another AI-anxiety take.

notes: Pool of 9 minus 4 content duplicates leaves exactly 5 unique fresh stories, all of which are picked. The final-5 outlet guard could not be satisfied: after dedup the only surviving outlets are Publishing Perspectives (3) and ALLi (2), and every under-represented-outlet alternative (404 Media x2, Good e-Reader, Jane Friedman) is a hard content duplicate. Dedup is the hard rule, so the guard yields rather than the dedup backstop. Three distinct story types are kept (litigation, regulation, rights economics / craft stance / technology roadmap) so category spread within the section still holds.
